items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: He was one of those guys who would just take chorus like Wild Bill Davison.

ctx.x: Smittie and Edgar went back to Cincinnati and I went to Paris for a week and played a job in that vicinity. I don't remember the name of this fellow that hired me or how much he paid me. The orchestra must have been amateurs the same as I, but it was the first time that I was paid to play music.

In those days a musician got work by word of mouth. Someone would speak about him, praising the way he played, so that if a band leader heard about it, he would hire you. Orchestras were getting bigger, because when I started to play, there were no more than six or seven pieces, but later on, they got to be nine or ten. I remember once in Cincinnati that the Alex Jackson band was visiting the city from New York. He wanted a trumpet player, and he asked me come and see him at his hotel. I was working with Wes…

I went home after the week was over but I had lost my job at Western Union, and my father was not happy about me staying away longer than I was supposed to and had no job when I came back. A trumpet player named Theodore Carpenter had left a carnival and was now playing with Clarence Page and I met him. Carpenter had only one arm having lost his left one in an accident somewhere on a machine that had pulled his arm off up to the shoulder. items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: He told me that his name was Bill Davison and he was the solo man in the Chubb Steinberg orchestra that was playing at Castle Farm... He blew a couple of numbers and then we talked together during the short rest.

ctx.x: I had not heard any white jazz musicians because negroes were not allowed to go to white dances, and they never went to those given by our people, although negro musicians were engaged to play white dances, private, public and in many of the white colleges.

This fellow really blew me out, which was not hard to do at that time, because I was still an amateur and he was a professional about my age. I found out later that he was 18 years old. I was 20. He blew a couple of numbers and then we talked together during the short rest. He told me that his name was Bill Davison and he was the solo man in the Chubb Steinberg orchestra that was playing at Castle Farm which was a big dance hall not far from Woodlawn Inn.

Bill Davison was born in a place called Defiance, Ohio, and was known as "Wild Bill" because he was able to drink a large quantity of alchohol at a very young age and I suppose he did some wild things as most young men do under the influence of alchohol.
